primitives.name: Fatigue Weight Fluctuation
primitives.verbatim_quote: There is a bad taste in the mouth and poor sleep, maybe persistent insomnia, and a failure to gain from day to day the weight rowed off.
primitives.assumptions: Daily weight variation is a proxy for metabolic stress; insomnia correlates with fatigue accumulation.
primitives.breakdown_regime: When \( W_{\text{gain/day}} < 0 \) and \( T_{\text{insomnia}} > 6 \) hours, recovery is insufficient.

layer2.mapping: Weight gain/loss trajectory maps to crew fatigue index via Bayesian regression in GSI; triggers state transition in GSE when deviation exceeds threshold.
layer2.telemetry: Daily body weight log, self-reported sleep duration

primitives.name: Recovery Protocol
primitives.verbatim_quote: The only treatment for this condition of fineness is rest, either partial or, if necessary, complete.
primitives.assumptions: Rest duration inversely affects fatigue index; dietary or environmental change improves recovery.
primitives.breakdown_regime: When \( R_{\text{rest}} < 3 \) days, fatigue persists beyond physiological limits.

layer2.mapping: Recovery protocol in GSE mirrors fatigue resolution in GSI through iterative feedback loops; both model recovery as a control variable.
layer2.telemetry: Duration of rest period, dietary modifications, relocation data

primitives.name: Stroke Rate Optimization
primitives.verbatim_quote: While in the barge the stroke should vary from 22 to 26 to the minute.
primitives.assumptions: Optimal stroke rate stabilizes muscle activation and reduces injury risk; transition to shell requires gradual increase.
primitives.breakdown_regime: If \( SR_{\text{barge}} > 26 \), risk of overexertion increases; if \( SR_{\text{shell}} < 22 \), efficiency drops.

layer2.mapping: Stroke rate in GSE is optimized using GSI-derived fatigue thresholds; transition from barge to shell modeled as phase shift in control system.
layer2.telemetry: Stroke rate during barge and shell phases, synchronization metrics

Fatigue weight fluctuation is a key indicator of metabolic stress, modeled as a stochastic process where daily weight gain/loss reflects muscular adaptation and recovery. Recovery protocols are formalized as control mechanisms—rest, diet, and environment changes—that act upon fatigue indices. Stroke rate optimization represents a dynamic control parameter, transitioning from barge to shell based on crew readiness. These operators form a dualistic framework: one side governs internal physiological states (fatigue, recovery), while the other governs external performance parameters (stroke rate, training schedule). Failure modes emerge when these systems decouple—e.g., insufficient rest leads to chronic fatigue, or improper stroke rate causes inefficiency. The interplay between these primitives enables a structured approach to training load management and crew performance prediction.
